name: Cirrus
description: Thin, wispy strands of ice crystals blown by high-altitude winds. Often the first sign of an approaching weather front. They appear bright white and hair-like against a blue sky.

name: Cirrocumulus
description: Small, white puffs arranged in rows or ripples, resembling fish scales. Composed entirely of ice crystals. Often called a 'mackerel sky' due to its pattern.

name: Cirrostratus
description: A thin, transparent sheet of ice crystals that covers much of the sky. Causes a halo effect around the sun or moon. Usually indicates rain or snow within 12–24 hours.

name: Altocumulus
description: Gray or white patches, sheets, or waves of cloud, larger than cirrocumulus puffs. Composed mainly of water droplets. Often seen on warm, humid mornings before afternoon thunderstorms.

name: Altostratus
description: A uniform, gray or blue-gray sheet that covers the sky. Thick enough to block the sun, producing a dull, overcast look. Associated with prolonged rain or snow.

name: Nimbostratus
description: A dark, thick, featureless cloud layer that produces continuous moderate-to-heavy precipitation. The cloud layer is so thick that sunlight rarely penetrates it.

name: Stratus
description: A low, uniform, gray layer that resembles fog. Produces drizzle or light rain. When it forms at ground level it is called fog. Associated with dull, grey days with little sunshine.

name: Stratocumulus
description: Low, lumpy patches or rolls of cloud, often in groups. The most common cloud type worldwide. Rarely produces significant rainfall. Appears in shades of white and gray.

name: Cumulus
description: Fluffy, white clouds with flat bases and dome-shaped tops. The classic 'fair weather' cloud when small, but can grow into storm clouds. Forms from rising thermal currents.

name: Cumulonimbus
description: Massive thunderstorm cloud that extends from low altitudes to the tropopause. Produces heavy rain, hail, lightning, and tornadoes. Characterized by an anvil-shaped top.
